name: AI in Prior Authorization
blurb: Automating approvals between providers and payers.
title: AI in Prior Authorization
answer: Prior authorization is a major administrative burden, and AI platforms now review requests against payer policy and approve many automatically. Federal rules are pushing the process onto electronic interfaces with set response times, which makes automation easier.

reading.body:
Prior authorization is being automated fastest where the payer, not the clinician, controls the interface. Federal rules now require electronic submission and faster decisions, and vendors claim most requests can clear without human review.

The pattern is that automation lands on the payer side of the transaction. A request is checked against written policy, which is a rules-matching problem, and rules-matching is what software does well. The 2024 CMS rule set response times and required electronic interfaces, which removes the fax-and-phone friction that made automation pointless before. Cohere Health's claimed 90 percent automatic approval rate is a vendor figure, not an audited one, but it describes the shape of the target.

For AI specifically, this is a governance story before it is a capability story. The published research runs from a 2019 paper on learning from patients' prior authorization history to 2025 and 2026 work on agentic workflows and large language models with rule-based coordination. The recurring concern in that literature is denial, not approval. An automated approval saves administrative cost. An automated denial shifts cost and risk onto a patient, and that is where the scrutiny sits.

What the data does not cover is how often automated decisions are overturned on appeal, how denial rates have moved, or whether any of these systems have been validated against clinical outcomes. It also does not establish that compute or power constrain this workload. Prior authorization is text and rules at modest scale, so the binding constraints here are policy and liability, not data centers.

The mechanism that makes prior authorization automatable is that the decision is already written down before the software sees it. Payer policy defines the criteria, the criteria map to fields in a request, and the software's job is to match fields to criteria. That is a retrieval and rules problem, not a reasoning problem, which is why the 2019 paper on learning from patients' historical authorization data sits in the same lineage as the 2026 work on large language models with rule-based workflow coordination. The models changed; the underlying task did not.

The comparison the data supports is between the two directions of an automated decision. An approval that clears without review removes a delay and a phone call. A denial that clears without review removes a clinician from a decision that determines whether a patient receives care, and the page's own guidance is to keep a clinician on every denial. The asymmetry is not about accuracy. It is about who absorbs the cost of an error, and the data shows the literature concentrating on denial for that reason.

The practical consequence for a care team is that the workflow change is mostly upstream of the denial. If most requests clear automatically, staff time shifts from assembling submissions to contesting the ones that do not, and the appeal becomes the new bottleneck. Nothing in the data measures appeal volume or overturn rates, so the size of that shift is unknown.

What is Cohere Health's claimed automatic approval rate?
Cohere Health says its platform can approve up to 90 percent of authorization requests automatically. The figure comes from the company's own announcement of a $90 million Series C, so it is a vendor claim rather than an audited result.

What did the 2024 CMS rule actually require?
CMS finalized an interoperability and prior authorization rule in January 2024 requiring payers to support electronic prior authorization and faster decisions. The data gives the requirement and the source but not the specific response-time thresholds.

Does the research show automated denials are more accurate or less accurate than human review?
The data does not hold an accuracy comparison. The papers listed cover ambient scribes and prior authorization platforms, ethics of using generative pretrained transformers for patient prior authorizations, learning from historical patient information, agentic workflows, and large language models with rule-based coordination, and none of them is described here as reporting denial accuracy.

How often are automated prior authorization decisions overturned on appeal?
The data does not contain appeal or overturn rates. It also does not show how denial rates have moved, so the effect of automation on either number cannot be read from this page.

Is prior authorization automation limited by compute or data center capacity?
No, and the data points the other way. The workload is text and rules at modest scale, so the constraints are policy and liability rather than compute or power.

Which vendors besides Cohere Health appear in this data?
Only Cohere Health is named among companies. Cohere also appears as a related company entry, and the data does not describe its role in prior authorization beyond that listing.
